messages.subject: MCMC/HMC refactor
parts:
Michael --- this all looks GREAT. Way better than the
way the code's currently organized. All the suggestions
below are very minor.

Michael is using a very different coding style than the
rest of Stan -- how much do we care about this kind of
thing? I'd volunteer to restyle it, but I don't want to
just do that unilaterally.

Here are some specific comments organized by file.

mcmc/mcmc_base.hpp
------------------
Break this file into two files, mcmc_sampler.hpp and sample.hpp
to follow the class defs.

What's the acceptance statistic and why is it part of a sample?
Isn't acceptance a property of a proposal sample relative to
a previous sample?

I'm ok with using "cont"/"disc" instead of "real"/"int",
but it should be consistent. (Yes, I realize it's all discrete
floating point reps underneath for reals, but Andrew 1 didn't
like "double", which is how I originally had it.)

mcmc/hmc_base.hpp
-----------------
Break out ps_point into its own file named ps_point.hpp
We're moving to finer grained and easier to navigate files
in the new math refactor, and I think it's a good idea.

Would it be useful to generalize away from teh normal
distribution for generating momenta? (I realize a fatter
tailed proposal doesn't help much, but it seems an easy
thing to generalize if it'll ever be needed for eval, etc.)

Looks like you got the RNG refs in there already.

mcmc/hamiltonian.hpp
--------------------
Break out into base_hamiltonian.hpp, unit_e_point.hpp,
and unit_metric.hpp.

What's the purpose of defining templated member functions
outside of the class? (And I didn't mean that question
rhetorically --- I'm genuinely curious.)

I can see the pain here with the std::vector to Eigen
conversion. Let's clean all that up next (which should be
a whole heckuva lot easier with this refactor).

What's with the empty comments at the bottom, like "DEFINE
HAMILTONIANS HERE"?

By the time this gets pushed, we should get rid of all commented
out code.


mcmc/chains.hpp
---------------
This doesn't look like it's changed much, but we should get rid of
that block of comments at the bottom. If they're to-do items,
they should go on the to-do list.

mcmc/adapter.hpp
----------------
stepsize_adapter class to file stepsize_adapter.hpp. (I'll let
you work out the rest of these moves).

This looks super clean compared to what we had before.

Do you really need setters or could you get away with a rich
constructor? I'd greatly prefer the latter because it's easier
to reason about the consistency of state with immutable objects.
Then you can get rid of the setters and make the member variables
private. If you do allow setters, there needs to be a check on
consistent values (such as some of these values being required
to be finite and positive).

mcmc/integrator.hpp
-------------------
Break into files named by class.

You can get rid of the protected: block in leapfrog -- there's
nothing in it. Ditto the private block of expl_leapfrog.


mcmc/hamiltonian.hpp
--------------------
Break into files named by class.

I think we should avoid mixing the underscore style and camel case,
so I'd rename "sampleP" to "sample_p" for consistency. (Overall,
the naming looks great and I take naming very seriously.)

Also some seemingly unanchored comments at the bottom.


mcmc/nuts.hpp
-------------
Break into files named by class.

These implementations look awesome.



In conclusion, I love the refactor. With this and what Daniel's
doing on the base math classes, this is all going to be a whole
lot easier to understand.

- Bob

On Thursday, March 28, 2013 3:28:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Michael --- this all looks GREAT.  Way better than the
way the code's currently organized.  All the suggestions
below are very minor.

I just wanted to ask a question: Is it possible to do the SoftMax thing based on the LDL' decomposition of the Hessian rather than the eigendecomposition? In either case, the determinant is just the product of the diagonal elements of the middle matrix, but I think the LDL' decomposition is faster than the (rather basic) self-adjoint eigendecomposition in Eigen. The only thing is that the former also does pivoting, so it is really a PLDL'P' decomposition where P is a permutation matrix that needs to be kept track of.

Ben

This was one place where I compromised because I didn't fully understand Boost's RNG and I couldn't imagine anyone trying non-quadratic kinetic energies anytime soon. I'd like to keep the Hamiltonians stateless, so would this be acceptable?

>> Conceptually, I don't think an acceptance probability is
>> part of a sample per se. As you point out, its interpretation
>> and contents is going to be very sampler specific. If we
>> had an exact sampler then there wouldn't even be an acceptance
>> statistic.

>> parameter configurations.
>>
>> There's also the issue of "sample" vs. potential sample.
>> And we wound up standardizing on "draw" in the external doc
>> because of the exact vs. MCMC sampling and the notion of
>> effective sample size.
>
> Yeah, sample doesn't really make sense -- we're talking about elements in a Markov chain. But in any case, we can always talk about an "acceptance statistic", even in the limit of independent samples when it asymptotes to 1.

This can lead to problematic designs. I did this in a few
places in the software for our company and it never failed
to trip users up (example: a probability method on text
spans that were sometimes extracted with a regex --- what
value do you give it so that users aren't confused?).
In this case, they'll run a regular sampler, get an object
with an "acceptance statistic" (your scare quotes, not mine!) and
wonder what it means.

The design obstacle is that for efficient C++ code, you don't want
any virtual methods (Java's all virtual all the time). That means
you have to write the code polymorphically (with templates) rather
than object oriented. The API problem of polymorphism is that
there's no within-the-language way to declare (as opposed to define
implicitly in whatever code uses the templates) what concepts are
required on the implementation of the class instantiating the
template.

In NUTS, we really have multiple acceptance
statistics --- there's the slicing then the sampling along
the path. That also argues for templating out the acceptance
stat. But then it becomes hard to use it when all different
classes implement it differently.

Anyway, you (Michael) are likely to be the one coding against
the API you're designing for the diagnostics.

>> Sure. See above -- we can always generalize later if
>> we need it. Boost's RNG isn't object oriented, it's
>> concept oriented, which is why you have to always template
>> out the RNG rather than provide some kind of base class
>> reference argument type.

> That's what I liked about RandomLib -- you passed the RNG by reference to each variate generator. Anyways, should be an easy enough fix.

messages.author: 6eae224f651d7e47
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] MCMC/HMC refactor
parts:
On Fri, Mar 29, 2013 at 8:26 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> The design obstacle is that for efficient C++ code, you don't want
> any virtual methods (Java's all virtual all the time).

Honestly, I think it's easy to get carried away here. On a decent and
a modern machine, virtual function calls overhead can be well under
three nanoseconds. Seriously (at least, if they're (dynamically)
predictable, which they are in this case, the branch predictor can do
perfectly well and the overhead is very, very hard to notice.)
Templating everything you do is not free; it makes code much harder to
read and follow, and is the primary cause of terrible compilation
times.

On my (fairly beefy) laptop, `make test-all` took something north of
48 hours. I really do recommend as part of the refactoring efforts
that we eliminate templates where they're not really necessary; if
you're avoiding a virtual function call, it better be something tiny,
inlined, and called more than once every, say, five hundred
instructions.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] MCMC/HMC refactor
parts:
On 3/29/13 1:44 PM, Andrew Hunter wrote:

> I really do recommend as part of the refactoring efforts
> that we eliminate templates where they're not really necessary; if
> you're avoiding a virtual function call, it better be something tiny,
> inlined, and called more than once every, say, five hundred
> instructions.

Sounds like a good idea.

We'd especially like to get model compilation time down because it's
often longer than the time to run a model. I'm less worried about
the libs and parser that get compiled once per version for users,
though it'd certainly be nice to speed that up for us developers.

More below.

> On Fri, Mar 29, 2013 at 8:26 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>> The design obstacle is that for efficient C++ code, you don't want
>> any virtual methods (Java's all virtual all the time).
>
> Honestly, I think it's easy to get carried away here.

I agree. Which is why I was suggesting we didn't do it
for this case. In this case, I don't even think we need
a virtual design yet.

Most of our templating is in order to support one of three
things:

a. specifying arguments that are written polymorphically
rather than with a suitable base class, such as the boost
RNGs,

b. dealing with the polymorphism presented by our different
scalars: double, stan::agrad::var, and soon, stan::agrad::fvar
for forward-mode auto-diff, and also by the vectorization of
functions where we use views, or

c. the polymorphism implicit in the Eigen matrix libs
and Boost math libs.

For b and c, we could get away with a bunch of overloaded
non-template functions on our sides. In some cases, like for
the probability functions, it'd be prohibitive (there are
literally hundreds of possible instantiations that could get
called in a model).

As for (c), the libraries we use are heavily templated, but
we only use a few instantiations underneath.

The design cost would be duplicated functions for different
types in some cases.

> On a decent and
> a modern machine, virtual function calls overhead can be well under
> three nanoseconds. Seriously (at least, if they're (dynamically)
> predictable, which they are in this case, the branch predictor can do
> perfectly well and the overhead is very, very hard to notice.)

And if the branch isn't predictable statically, we can't
template it away anyway!

> Templating everything you do is not free; it makes code much harder to
> read and follow, and is the primary cause of terrible compilation
> times.
>
> On my (fairly beefy) laptop, `make test-all` took something north of
> 48 hours.

48 hours? Yikes. Our observation is that if you parallelize (-j4 on
my recent generation Macbook Pro with four cores), the tests take
about the following amounts of time:

basic unit tests: 5 minutes

distribution unit tests: 20 minutes

model functional tests: 60 minutes

That's running everything -O3. The model tests can take longer
run at lower optimization.

We have a buildbot set up to do continuous tests, but the model tests
and distribution tests are now set up to run daily rather than versus
every change in the code base.

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] MCMC/HMC refactor
parts:
As Ben has mentioned, using clang++ is much faster. And g++ 4.6 is going to be faster than 4.2. I'm actually surprised it all compiled with g++ 4.2.

I think I told Bob the wrong numbers earlier. Especially after the refactoring, but it definitely shouldn't take 48 hours.

With regards to test targets, we have:
* test-unit: the unit tests (excluding distribution tests, unless they've already been generated) ~1100 tests
* test-distribution: the distribution tests. We've got ~180k tests here.
* test-models: tests the models we have built against known values. We use these to make sure our end-to-end process still works as well as verifying that our sampling is still returning reasonable values. Our unit tests do test whether or not code is being generated properly, but this really focuses on the results from sampling.
* test-all: just calls the above targets.

We usually stick to running the unit-tests while developing. If we're playing with distributions, we'll also run the distribution tests. The model tests should be run if you're playing with samplers, derivatives of distributions, etc. But for the most part, we rely on our continuous integration server to tell us whether the models are broken. You can see the results here:
http://d1m1s1b1.stat.columbia.edu:8080/




Daniel

Great. Let us know what you're untemplatizing and how.
(Not to check your work, but so we can see how to do it
better next time.)

The only issue I know of ahead of time is that we need to make
sure not to lose instantiations for alternative scalar types
where we don't have appropriate specializations.

Another issue where we've been toying with simplifying dramatically
is in error handling policy arguments. They're everywhere in
our distributions, and either need to get pushed into our
math libs so that they also have configurable behavior, or simply
removed. The reason we haven't done this yet is that we know
some styles, like Google's, frown on exceptions, yet we're using
them to signal error conditions and locations in a way that would
be very very inconvenient to do any other way.

Although the grammars are only compiled once, I think
the top-level classes could be hardcoded for the iterator
type that's templated everywhere. Otheter than that, I'm curious
what can be untemplated.

- Bob
